text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes develops slowly, and many people have no obvious symptoms in the early stages.

list.snippet: Frequent urination: Needing to pee more often—especially at night—happens as your kidneys try to flush out extra sugar from your blood.
Increased thirst and dry mouth: High blood sugar pulls fluid from your tissues, leaving you unusually thirsty even after drinking.
Constant fatigue: When your cells cannot properly absorb glucose for energy, you feel persistently tired and worn out.
Blurry vision: High blood sugar can cause temporary fluid swelling in the lenses of your eyes.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: Elevated blood sugar impairs circulation and your immune system's ability to heal wounds.
Tingling or numbness: Peripheral nerve damage can cause a burning or prickling sensation, or loss of feeling, in your hands and feet.
Unexplained weight changes: Your body may lose weight unexpectedly if it starts burning fat and muscle for energy, or experience weight gain linked to insulin resistance.
Frequent infections: Higher sugar levels encourage the growth of bacteria and fungi, leading to common skin, gum, or urinary tract infections.
Darkened skin patches: Velvety, dark patches around the neck, armpits, or groin (acanthosis nigricans) can be a sign of insulin resistance.

text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using simple blood tests through a healthcare provider, such as a fasting plasma glucose test or an A1C test (which measures your average blood sugar over the past two to three months).
You can learn more about diagnostic criteria and guidelines at the Cleveland Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Guide or review clinical overviews from the Mayo Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Page.
